title: Why do we lift?
summary: An unscripted love letter to lifting. NH says people lift to change a body they hate, to gain confidence and attractiveness, to become more useful and harder to prey on, and to improve their health and mental health. He calls lifting an anti-modern ritual that ties lifters to their physically active ancestors and ends with lifters becoming their own role models.
claims: Lifting is a cheap hobby; supplements, special programs and diet plans are superfluous, and people built great physiques 50-60 years ago without them
At 14-15 NH hated his body so much that he hid under coats and grew his hair long and greasy to cover his face
Waking up in a body you love matters more than anything, and many people's unhappiness comes from living in a body that doesn't feel like home
NH can't pinpoint when he started feeling good about his body; stop asking when you will get there and let the process possess you
Asking whether lifting is worth it is pointless, because the time would otherwise be wasted on unproductive things
Lifting teaches through the body that you can change; after six months of work you see the proof
Starting to lift to attract women is legitimate; women like muscle mainly because it signals hard work, commitment and physical capability
Women have told NH his physique was too much, and he doesn't care because it is his vision
Lifting only to please women leads to a mediocre Fight Club-type physique and quitting; people who lift for themselves stick with it
Pride is essential: the healthy middle between self-deprecation and narcissism sits closer to narcissism than society admits
Showing your results gives others permission and proof that they can do it too
You cannot buy a big body without steroids, which makes lifting anti-modern; staying natural keeps it pure
Lifting never lies or betrays you: you get out what you put in
NH believes lifting is the single best thing for mental health; the barbell-as-therapist meme is true
He agrees with Rippetoe that lifters are more useful people and harder to kill
An untrained man deadlifts maybe 200 lb, while any lifter can reach 400 lb, so lifters are about twice as strong
Lifting lowers blood pressure and the risk of cancer, diabetes and heart attacks, and makes you more resilient to accidents
NH has heard of a man in a T-bone crash whose neck muscles absorbed the shock, leaving him with a strained neck instead of a broken one
Lifting floods you with dopamine and endorphins; NH feels he can now trigger good feelings at will, and lifting helps depression and anxiety
Lifting reduces your need for approval, which makes you more socially at ease
If everyone lifted, most of society's problems, from obesity to mental illness, would largely disappear
Pain is just a sensation; lifting teaches that everything worth doing is hard
Lifting teaches personal responsibility and agency
When skinny NH was bullied into constant fights; since getting big he hasn't had to fight in 6-7 years
Kindness only counts as virtue if you could be a tyrant; become strong, then choose to be kind
Lifting is a ritual close to religion that reconnects you with ancestors who did physical labor; this is the first generation that knows nothing of physical labor
NH's 92-year-old grandfather, a construction worker since 14 and a field worker since 9, still walks his fields for 3 hours from 5 a.m. and carried a felled tree at 90
Lifting builds the muscle mass you carry into old age so you stay active
Removing all struggle makes people miserable; life works like progressive overload, so embrace struggle
NH can't go more than two days without lifting before his body aches; five days off would drive him insane
Taking a six-month break from lifting is taking a break from happiness and mental stability
Lifting lets you become your own power fantasy; NH no longer needs manga for motivation, and having become a role model you should give back
